source.title: Scaling End-to-End Models for Large-Scale Multilingual ASR
source.authors: Bo Li; Ruo-Ming Pang; T. Sainath; Anmol Gulati; Yu Zhang; James Qin; Parisa Haghani; W. R. Huang; Min Ma; Junwen Bai

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies multilingual speech-recognition model capacity, but does not test the claim’s language-model loss laws, power-law extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. It cites Kaplan et al. when contextualizing its own training-efficiency observation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASR word-error-rate and training-efficiency results as model capacity changes. These do not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss or establish a power-law fit, so the related ASR scaling findings are recorded under fits_no_version. The Kaplan et al. result is cited, not independently tested.
record.test_reason: The study scales multilingual ASR encoder-decoder models (220M to 10B) and reports WER and training efficiency at four or five sizes. It fits no power law, measures no held-out language-model pretraining loss, and does no compute-optimal or extrapolation analysis. Kaplan et al. is cited only for the sample-efficiency analogy and the width/depth split. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Scaling capacity up to 10B gives consistent but small WER gains and better sample and TPU-time efficiency. The multilingual model beats monolingual baselines on most high-resource languages. Remaining lags (e.g. Russian) are attributed to data imbalance. Models can be extended to new languages and domains by continued training.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales end-to-end multilingual ASR models and evaluates WER and training efficiency; it does not use the original language-model loss-scaling measurement or fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that model depth versus width, encoder versus decoder capacity, language data mixing, and the training setup affect ASR results.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 220M to 10B multilingual ASR models, average WER falls from 9.43% to 9.04%. The gain from 1B to 10B is described as marginal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In large-scale multilingual ASR, WER improves with model size, with diminishing gains from 1B to 10B parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger ASR models reach a given WER in fewer steps and fewer TPU days (1B at 34% of the 500M model's time). Authors liken this to Kaplan et al.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger ASR models are more sample- and training-cost-efficient, as in LM scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 compares roughly 1B-parameter variants at 200K steps. Training loss ranges 0.143 to 0.158 and WER 10.05% to 10.48%. Deeper beats wider, and encoder capacity helps WER more than decoder capacity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ASR encoder-decoder models at fixed size, depth/width and encoder/decoder allocation change WER and loss modestly but noticeably.

record.problems: The reported results relevant to scaling use ASR WER and training efficiency, not held-out language-model loss; no uncertainty estimates are stated for these results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Other reported comparisons concern ASR architecture, language balancing, language expansion, or domain transfer rather than the claim’s specified measurements.

untested.parts: No held-out LM pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from fitted small-run laws.
Width/depth ablations exist, but for ASR models, not language models. Not tested for the system the version names.
ASR is a non-text setting, but no power-law form is fitted or tested. There are only a handful of sizes, with WER as the measure.
No relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss or a fitted scale trend for LMs.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal split to compare across setups.

missing.what: Table 2 width/depth and encoder/decoder ablations at about 1B parameters (training loss and WER). This is relevant context for a researcher comparing with V4, though for ASR rather than LMs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/cites_only call stands. Kaplan [29] is cited for the sample-efficiency observation and the equal width/depth split. The study does not test scaling laws.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its trend with compute.
Whether architecture details change held-out language-model loss only slightly at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds beyond text pretraining; the study reports ASR WER results but does not fit or test power laws.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: 500M-param model
rows.operation_detail: Increased multilingual ASR model capacity; reported average WER at convergence.
rows.note: ASR WER is not held-out language-model pretraining loss and does not establish a power-law relationship.
rows.check: ASR WER for an LSTM-decoder 500M model. It is not language-model loss and has no power-law fit. Values (9.13% vs 9.29%) are correct.

rows.subject: E3 1B-param model
rows.operation_detail: Scaled the multilingual ASR model; reported average WER at convergence.
rows.note: The paper reports the ASR outcome, not a held-out language-model loss or a power-law fit.
rows.check: ASR WER for the E3 1B model (9.07%). Correct, but it bears on no version.

rows.subject: 10B-param model
rows.operation_detail: Scaled the multilingual ASR model; reported average WER.
rows.note: The authors describe the WER gain over the 1B model as marginal. This ASR result does not determine whether language-model loss follows a power law.
rows.check: ASR WER for the 10B model (9.04% at 330K steps). Authors call the gain over 1B marginal. Bears on no version.

rows.subject: 1B-param model
rows.operation_detail: Compared training time required to reach the same accuracy as the 500M-param model.
rows.measure: training time relative to the 500M-param model
rows.note: This is a training-efficiency comparison, not a test of language-model compute-optimal allocation or a power-law loss relation.
rows.check: Training-cost efficiency (34% of TPU time to match the 500M model). It is not a compute-optimal allocation test.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
